questions.explanation: The service has a budget, and every request spends some of it whether or not it is hostile. A well-formed request costs parsing, a handler, a response, a connection slot and a slice of the second the worker held, and the ratio of that cost to the value returned is a property of the service's design rather than of the sender. Once the arrival rate exceeds the rate at which the service can retire work, the queue in front of the workers grows, every later request waits behind everything already there, and the observable effect on a real user is that a correct answer arrives too late to use. Nothing has to be wrong with any single request, and nothing in the application's own logs says so, because every entry in those logs reads as a successful request. This is why saturation is treated as a security topic and not only a capacity topic: the same request, repeated at a rate the design did not anticipate, is a denial of service that no input filter will catch, because there is nothing in the input to filter. It also changes what detection should look for. A rule that watches for malformed input is watching for the wrong signature. What is worth alerting on is arrival rate, queue depth, and the ratio of completed work to accepted work, because those three move together during a flood and stay flat during every other kind of incident. The first distractor holds that correct behaviour is the same as availability, which is true of one request and false of ten thousand. The third treats saturation as a data integrity event, which would require the service to be computing from inconsistent state and nothing here requires that. The last one places the loss below the service, when the service is precisely what has been consumed.

questions.explanation: The routing decision is the whole mechanism, and everything else is bookkeeping. A reply is not sent back to whoever asked the question; it is sent back to the source address carried in the request as it arrived. A sender that cannot choose that address can only aim its own traffic at itself, which is a small amount of traffic spread over a large number of machines and is not an attack worth running. A sender that can choose it sends a modest request from the victim's address to a service that replies generously, and the reply is delivered to the victim rather than to the sender. The attacker therefore pays for the request and somebody else pays for the response, and the ratio between the two is the difference between a small query and a large answer. That is why services which answer questions that can be made larger than the question are worth knowing about: an open name resolver that will return a full record set converts a cheap outbound packet into an expensive inbound one aimed wherever the sender chose. The defensive side has three moves and they are worth separating. One is to make the reply no larger than the request, which removes the ratio at source and is the only fix that helps other people's networks as well as your own. The second is to refuse requests from ranges that should never be asking, which is effective against reflection and useless against a direct flood. The third is to absorb the excess, which is what a scrubbing service or a larger transit pipe is for. The first distractor identifies the reply size, which is a necessary property of the technique but not the thing that aims it, since a service replying at exactly the size it was asked still reflects to the address in the request. The second says the address must be known in advance, which is false because the attacker chooses it. The last one assumes the victim consents, and a reflection victim does not know it is happening.
questions.hint: Ask where a reply is delivered, and who chooses that address.

questions.explanation: The asymmetry is in the unit cost, and it is the reason the technique scales in the attacker's favour. A sender that emits a small packet pays for that small packet's worth of link capacity and nothing more; the cost of the reply is paid by the intermediate service that emits it and by the victim's uplink that receives it. If the reply is a fixed large multiple of the request, the attacker multiplies its own outbound cost by that factor without multiplying its own bill, and the binding constraint becomes the availability of the sending capacity rather than the cost of the attack. A defender in the same position is in the opposite arithmetic. Every byte that arrives has to be received off a link, counted, filtered, and either forwarded or discarded, and that work happens before anyone can decide the packet is unwanted. A link that is saturated is already failing, and no filter sitting behind it can restore the capacity it has consumed. This is why the practical answer is more bandwidth rather than a smarter filter, which sounds defeatist and is the correct diagnosis: a filter reduces the forwarded volume, and the arriving volume is what the bottleneck is measured against. Two corollaries matter for planning. The attacker's cost rises slowly while the defender's rises immediately, so the attack is profitable at sizes where the defence is not yet economic. And the target's own provider sees the traffic as inbound, which makes it easy to misclassify as ordinary load growth unless the arrival pattern is examined. The first distractor names a real cost but not the binding one, because filtering cost is paid on the link that is already full. The third asserts an accounting exemption that does not exist for an inbound flood. The last one claims the target's hardware is irrelevant, which confuses the arrival path with the processing path.

questions.explanation: There are two different queues in front of the work, and they fail in different ways, so a control aimed at the wrong one gives the appearance of protection while the service stays unavailable. The first holds connections that have started but not finished their handshake. A server can bound it, and the standard defence does something more elegant: it declines to store anything, encodes the state it would have needed into a value the client has to send back, and only then commits. The second holds connections that are fully established and waiting for a worker thread. Nothing about a handshake can stop a client completing it, and nothing about a client means the request will ever be served, so this is the queue where a service accumulates work it has accepted and cannot do. When it is full the connection is normally closed and the client sees a refusal. The failure mode is specific and worth naming: the service is not down, its own health page answers, and its accept count keeps rising, while the fraction of clients that receive an answer falls steadily. That is why a health check which only asks whether the process is running will keep reporting success, and why queue depth and the ratio of accepted to completed connections are more informative than process liveness. The first distractor refuses the idea that an accepted connection can be declined, which is a confusion between the handshake and the request. The third is the classic reflection of the correct answer onto the wrong queue, and it is the one people reach for first because the handshake table is the one classically attacked. The last one mistakes a limit on a queue for a limit on a resource: bounding a queue bounds how many connections wait, not how many threads exist.

questions.explanation: The cap is a per-source limit, so its protective value and its blind spot both follow from that one word. What it removes is the cheapest and most common way to stop a service: one machine opening a very large number of connections and letting them sit. That costs the target a connection slot, a slot in the accept queue, and often memory for buffers attached to the connection, and a single host can consume a disproportionate share of all three. With the cap in place that host reaches its ceiling and the service remains usable by everyone else. What the cap does not do is bound anything about the total, because the sum over all source addresses is unbounded and an attacker controlling a wide range of addresses can still open the allowed number from each. That is a real limit on the defence and not a defect in it, because the alternative to a per-source cap is no cap at all. The practical response is to layer it: a global cap on total connections, a short timeout on connections that never send a request, and a limit on the rate at which new connections are accepted, which bounds the rate at which the queue can be filled even when its depth is not directly limited. questions.explanation: The defence works by changing where the state lives, and it is effective because the state the server needs is small enough to fit in the value the client has to return. What a server normally does is allocate a record when a connection begins and hold it until the connection completes or times out. Under a flood of connection starts, that record allocation is the exhaustible resource: the attacker never has to complete anything, and the server's table fills with entries for conversations that were never going to happen. A value carried in the handshake reverses that. The server computes a short string from a secret it holds and from the details of the request, sends it, and keeps nothing. The client has to return it, and a client that is not finishing a conversation never reaches the point of returning anything, so the only cost the attacker achieves is one small value in flight. When the client does return it, the server verifies the value, recovers the state from it, and only then allocates. Nothing about the verification is secret from the client; the point is that a client can produce the value only by receiving it, and receiving it means it is participating. The costs are real and worth stating. A stateless scheme cannot carry an arbitrary amount of state, so it carries a compact encoding and a short validity, which makes the defence weaker for connections that legitimately take a long time to complete. It also keeps no memory of recent bad actors, so an address that keeps failing verification is treated like a new one. The first distractor overstates the result into a complete barrier, which it is not. The second names the stateful variant, which does help but pays for the help in exactly the resource under attack. The last one describes a bandwidth effect, and the defence is about server state rather than link capacity.

questions.explanation: Stateful inspection is bought with memory, and that memory is per connection rather than per rule. To know that an arriving packet belongs to a conversation already permitted, the device has to have recorded something about that conversation: its addresses, its ports, its state, and often a timer. That record is what lets it distinguish return traffic from a new connection attempt, and it is also what an attacker consumes when the device is fed connection starts. Once the table is full the device has three bad options and no good ones. It can refuse to create new entries, in which case legitimate new connections are treated as unsolicited and dropped, and the protected service becomes unreachable. It can evict something, in which case whichever conversation was evicted has its return traffic reclassified as a new connection and the same thing happens later. Or it can allocate beyond its limit, in which case it begins to swap and the device that exists to protect the network becomes the slowest thing on it. All three outcomes are availability failures, and none is visible in the rule set, which is why an exhausted state table is so often misdiagnosed as a policy problem. The defences that actually help are the ones that stop entries being created: a value in the handshake so the device need not track an incomplete connection, timeouts short enough that abandoned conversations do not sit in the table, a deliberate decision about what happens when the entry cap is reached, and filters that drop obviously unwanted connection starts before the tracking layer ever sees them. The first distractor assumes a full table is protective, which inverts the situation. The second treats eviction as free, when it moves the cost onto existing conversations. The last one confuses a per-connection state table with a cache of decisions, which is the wrong mental model and produces the wrong fixes.

questions.explanation: The two limiters differ in what they treat as the thing being controlled. The token bucket treats the rate as a long-run property and the burst as something the client is entitled to spend whenever it has been quiet. It holds a counter of available allowance, adds to it at the sustained rate up to a ceiling, and removes from it on every request. A client that has sent nothing for an hour arrives to find the counter full and can therefore send the whole ceiling in a moment, after which it is limited to the sustained rate for as long as it keeps going. The sustained rate is respected over any window long enough to average out, and the burst capability is a deliberate feature, because real traffic is bursty and a limiter that punishes a client for a legitimate burst will simply be worked around. The leaky bucket treats the rate as something that must hold in every interval. Requests go into a queue of bounded length and leave it at the sustained rate regardless of when they arrived, so the client is shaped rather than refused and the total volume is preserved at the cost of delay. The difference matters when what is being protected is a downstream service with a specific concurrency limit: a token bucket lets a hundred idle clients all arrive at once at the moment the downstream recovers, and a leaky bucket spreads that same hundred out. The practical answer is usually both, at different layers. The first distractor names the leaky bucket and attributes the burst allowance to it, which is exactly backwards. The third describes a fixed window, whose boundary problem is a separate defect rather than a burst allowance. The last one describes a sliding window, which is a memory cost paid for precision rather than a permission to burst.

questions.explanation: Shaping and counting are different jobs, and a leaky bucket is a shaper. The arithmetic makes the distinction concrete: the client sent 600 requests against a contract of 10 a second, so 590 of them are in excess, and the question is what happens to the excess. A leaky bucket has a queue of bounded length, and the excess goes into that queue. From then on the queue drains at 10 a second, so those 590 requests are answered over the following 59 seconds and the client's request is not dropped, it is delayed. Two things follow, and both are why the mechanism exists. The service is protected, because the instantaneous rate at which work arrives is 10 a second no matter what the client did. The client's total volume is preserved, which matters because for most callers the request is not optional, and silently discarding it produces a retry, a support call and a worse experience than a delay. The cost of the mechanism is exactly that delay, and it grows without limit if the queue is unbounded, which is why a real implementation bounds the queue and then either drops the newest arrivals or closes the connection when the bound is reached. A token bucket behaves differently with the same input: its allowance refills at 10 a second, and a client idle for 59 seconds has accumulated enough to send 590 in a burst, so the excess is neither delayed nor discarded but spent immediately. A fixed counter answers the question how many requests have arrived since the top of the clock minute, and it has no memory of anything before that instant. Two bursts on either side of a boundary are therefore judged against two different counters, each empty when its burst arrives, and the client's total across the boundary is twice the intended rate. This is a design fault rather than an implementation bug, and it survives so long because it is invisible in any test whose load is uniform: uniform load never puts two bursts near a boundary, so the counter is never observed empty twice in quick succession. It becomes visible exactly when traffic is bursty, which is most of the time. The fix is either to track arrival times individually, so the limiter can say precisely how many of the last 60 seconds this is, or to add a second counter that is halved rather than cleared at each boundary, which removes the worst of the doubling at the cost of a small permanent over-permit. questions.explanation: The sliding window log is the only common limiter that can answer the question the contract actually asks, which is how many of the last 60 seconds this is. It does that by remembering, for each request, when it arrived, and by discarding any record that has fallen out of the window. A request is allowed exactly when the number of surviving records is below the limit, so the boundary case that defeats the fixed counter cannot arise: a request at two seconds after the boundary still sees the 100 records that arrived before it. Memory is proportional to the number of requests inside the window, not to the number of clients and not to the limit, so a single client sending at exactly the limit consumes the limit's worth of records continuously, and a client sending ten times the limit is refused before its extra requests are ever recorded. That is usually acceptable, and it is worth knowing that the refusal path and the record path are different, so a client that is being refused still costs almost nothing. Two cheaper approximations exist and both are widely used. A sliding window counter keeps a small fixed number of buckets and interpolates between them, which gives a slightly wrong answer near a boundary and costs constant memory. A fixed counter with a decaying second counter costs less still and permits somewhat more than intended near a boundary. questions.explanation: The limit is counted in the wrong place, and moving the counter to the right place is the whole of the fix. A per-account counter bounds how fast one account may attempt sign-ins, which is exactly the right control for a caller who has one account and is guessing one person's password. It stops that caller after 10 attempts in a minute and it does so regardless of how many other accounts exist, because the counter it fills is the one belonging to the account being attacked. An attacker who signs up for 40 accounts is not making 40 attempts against one account; they are making one attempt from each of 40 accounts, and each is judged by a different counter that was at zero. The rate the victim experiences is the sum across the attacker's accounts, so the per-account limit is fully satisfied at every instant while the protection it was supposed to provide is absent. The general lesson is that a limit is only as good as the identity it is keyed on, and a sign-in system contains two identities: the party making the request and the party being targeted. Which to key on depends on what is being protected. Keying on the caller is right when the cost being protected is per caller, which covers automated traffic and volume attacks in general. Keying on the target is right when the cost being protected is a single victim's exposure to guessing, and that limit has to count failures against the account being targeted and has to survive the count being cleared by a success. The first distractor says the victim's own account is the one being limited, which inverts which counter is consulted. The third claims a successful sign-in clears the target's count, which is a different design. The last one claims the limit is applied to the target, which is the correct design and not the one in the stem.

questions.explanation: A queue buys nothing about time, and that is the property that matters once arrival rate exceeds service rate. If work arrives faster than it can be retired, the backlog grows by the difference on every interval, so the time a request waits is set by how long the queue has been growing and not by anything the service does afterwards. A caller that needed an answer in 200 milliseconds now waits for however long the backlog is, and no amount of correct processing changes that. Rejecting a share immediately converts the same overload into a bounded wait for the requests that are accepted and an immediate, unambiguous failure for the ones that are not. That is a better user experience than an unbounded wait, because a caller can act on a fast error: retry elsewhere, queue on the client, show a message, fall back to a degraded mode. It is also a better operator experience, because the service is answering most callers in a predictable time instead of answering everyone eventually at an unpredictable time. What is given up has to be said plainly, because it is a real loss and not a trick. Rejected work is work the caller wanted, and if the caller retries, the retry adds to the arrival rate. That is why shedding has to be paired with a signal telling the caller not to retry immediately, and why a rejected request is cheaper than a queued one. It is also why the choice of what to shed matters: shedding cheap requests protects expensive ones, and shedding long-running work protects the short requests that keep the service looking alive. The first distractor says a queue is strictly better, which holds only while the queue is not growing. The third says rejection saves the caller nothing, which is the opposite of the reason to do it. The last one describes bounding memory, a real benefit of a bounded queue but not the one that distinguishes shedding from holding.
questions.hint: Ask what sets the waiting time when arrivals exceed the service rate.

questions.explanation: A cascade is a chain in which each link's slowness is somebody else's arrival rate, and a bound on one link's queue breaks the chain at that link by making the excess visible immediately instead of eventually. Without a bound, service A keeps accepting work for service B as long as its own memory lasts, so A's callers wait, and A's queue is now part of the problem rather than a buffer for it. B may be recovering perfectly well and still be unable to help, because A is presenting it with a backlog accumulated over minutes rather than a request rate. With a bound, A holds a fixed number of requests and refuses the rest at once. That refusal is the pressure moving upstream to A's callers, which is where it can be dealt with: by a client that backs off, by a limit at the edge, or by a visible error rate. The bound also caps A's exposure to B's recovery time, because when B comes back it finds a small queue to work through rather than a large one, and a service that has been down for a minute does not spend its first second of health rebuilding a backlog accumulated before it returned. What the bound does not do is make the underlying slowness disappear, and it is worth being clear that the failure has moved rather than been solved. Two related designs are worth distinguishing. A bounded queue that blocks puts back-pressure on the caller by holding its thread, which protects the queue and spends a resource to do it. A bounded queue that refuses is cheaper and reports the condition. The first distractor says the bound removes the growth without noting where the growth goes, which is the whole mechanism. The third assumes a silent discard, which is a different policy and one that loses work. The last one claims the bound limits what B receives, confusing a local queue bound with a global rate limit on the dependency.

questions.explanation: Retries are load. A retry is a fresh request with the full cost of the original one, and the condition that provokes it is usually a server that is already degraded, so the retries arrive precisely when there is least capacity to absorb them. An unbounded loop with no pause turns that into a positive feedback loop: the server gets slower, more callers time out, more callers retry immediately, the server gets slower again. The rate at which the loop sends is the rate at which the client can generate requests, which is typically far above the rate the service can retire them, so a service that would have recovered from a two-second fault instead spends its recovery window saturated. Every component of the fix matters and they are not interchangeable. A bound on the number of attempts caps the total load a single caller can add. A pause between attempts reduces the instantaneous rate. Randomising that pause stops every client that failed at the same moment from retrying at the same moment, which is the difference between spreading a spike and reproducing it. Retrying only the failures that are plausibly transient, rather than every error, stops the loop amplifying the errors that retrying cannot fix. And a caller that has exhausted its attempts has to tell somebody, because a silent client and a user who has given up produce the same absence of traffic and are very different incidents. The mistake this prevents is a specific one: treating the retry as free because it is the same call. The first distractor has the direction of causation backwards. The third says the service does no extra work, which would be true of a deduplicated request and is not true of a retry. The last one claims the client's throughput improves, when a retry against a service that has already failed returns the same failure sooner rather than making progress.

questions.explanation: The problem the scheme has to solve is not that clients wait, it is that they wait in unison. Thousands of clients talking to one service fail together whenever the service stumbles, because the failure is shared: one restart, one network blip, one deployment takes them all down at the same instant. With a pure doubling schedule every one of them waits one second, then every one of them tries again in the same second, then two seconds, then four. The result is a series of synchronised spikes whose peak rate is the entire client population rather than a small fraction of it, which is the opposite of what backoff was supposed to produce. The pause length is therefore the wrong place to intervene: making the delays longer spreads the same population over a longer period without reducing the peak. What works is breaking the alignment. A random offset, drawn per client and per attempt and bounded by the current delay, means the clients are no longer on a shared clock, so their attempts distribute across the interval instead of landing in it together. This is usually described as jitter and it composes with everything else: the exponential growth still gives each client an individually increasing pause, the cap still bounds the worst case, and the random component makes the population's aggregate arrival rate roughly uniform. Its limits are worth stating. Jitter does not reduce the total number of attempts, so an attempt cap is still needed, and it does not help a single client, for whom the delays are simply longer on average. The first distractor says the doubling is the problem and proposes a variable multiplier, which would leave the clients sharing a schedule. The second and third both pick the wrong quantity, one the attempt count and one the population size, neither of which is what the change addresses.

questions.explanation: A dependency does not fail cleanly and it does not recover cleanly, and a two-state switch cannot represent the middle of that. Consider what the caller needs to know. When the dependency is healthy it should pass traffic through. When it is clearly down, calling it is pointless and the failure is fast, so the caller should stop. Between those two states is the case that dominates in practice: the dependency is coming back, or it is intermittently failing, and a small amount of traffic will succeed while a large amount will not. That is what the third state exists for. With the breaker open the caller stops calling. A timer expires, and the breaker admits a small controlled number of trial calls while every other call is refused or served from a fallback. If the trials succeed the breaker closes and full traffic resumes; if they fail it opens again for another interval. This turns an unbounded recovery problem into a bounded experiment, and it is the difference between a service discovering that its dependency is back within a few seconds and one that rediscovers it whenever enough callers happen to fail through. The design details that matter are the number of trial calls, the success threshold, and the interval, and they interact: too many trial calls and the experiment is itself a flood, too few and a dependency that is 90 per cent healthy reads as dead. A saved response can be served instead of an error, which is what makes the scheme usable on read paths, and that is a real decision rather than a free win, because a stale response has to be labelled as one. The first distractor models the dependency as a switch. The second and third both misdescribe the third state, one as immediate retries and one as a plain delay, and the middle state is neither.

questions.explanation: A liveness question is the cheapest question a load balancer can ask, and cheapest is exactly why it is the default. It establishes that the process is there and that the network path to it works, which is the minimum needed to keep a node in rotation at all. It says nothing about whether the instance can complete the work it is about to be sent, and the gap between those two things is where the most damaging misconfiguration lives. An instance whose worker pool is fully occupied, whose outbound dependency is timing out, whose memory is exhausted and swapping, or whose database connection pool is empty will answer a liveness question perfectly and fail every real request. The load balancer will keep sending it work, so the service's overall success rate falls while every individual instance looks healthy. That is why a liveness check which asks whether the process is running is the right default and the wrong measure, and why the two are worth distinguishing: liveness answers should tell the platform whether to restart the process, while readiness answers tell the load balancer whether to send it work, and the questions should be different because the decisions are different. A readiness check that depends on the downstream store will remove an instance during a downstream outage, which is sometimes right and sometimes catastrophic depending on whether the instance can serve anything at all without it. The practical discipline is to make readiness reflect whether this instance can serve now, to keep liveness cheap so it can run often, and to watch the ratio of accepted to completed requests precisely because neither probe reports it. The first distractor treats liveness as a complete statement of capacity. The second claims the load balancer has an independent view of capacity, which it does not. The last one says the gap must be closed by asking the instance rather than by observing the effect of saturation.

questions.explanation: The cost asymmetry between a hit and a miss is what turns an ordinary expiry into an outage, and it is worth quantifying because the ratio is often three orders of magnitude. A cache hit is a lookup: a key comparison and a return, with no call out to the thing being cached. A miss is a lookup plus the entire operation the cache exists to avoid, which for a common case means a query, a remote call, or a computation over a large data set. Now put concurrency on top of that. In steady state a hot key is a hit for nearly every caller, so nearly every caller pays the cheap path and the origin sees a small fraction of the traffic. At the instant the entry expires, the entry is gone for everyone simultaneously, so every caller in flight and every caller arriving during the recomputation pays the expensive path, and the origin sees a spike proportional to its own throughput rather than to the miss rate it is used to. The recomputation takes long enough that many callers arrive during it, which is the part that makes it self-sustaining: the longer the expensive path takes, the more callers pile onto it. There are three ways out and each trades something. Serving the stale entry while one caller refreshes keeps latency near the hit cost and makes the data briefly old. Widening the time-to-live reduces how often the event happens without removing it. Capping the work per refresh, for instance recomputing from a cheaper source, bounds the duration of the spike. None of them is free, and the design decision is a choice about how stale the value is allowed to be. The first distractor says the total work is unchanged, which ignores the miss cost entirely. The third assumes a write happens before the next read, which is exactly what does not happen during the gap. The second describes a stampede and calls it a recovery.
questions.hint: Ask what one miss costs compared with one hit, and who pays it at the same time.

questions.explanation: The change serialises the expensive part rather than removing it, and the risk it introduces is the mirror image of the problem it solves. Before the change, every concurrent caller for a missing key did its own computation, so the origin saw one expensive operation per caller and the stampede was a function of how many callers were in flight. After the change, the first caller to find the key missing takes a lock for that key and computes. Every other caller that arrives for the same missing key waits for that one result instead of starting its own. The origin now sees one expensive operation per key rather than one per caller, and the cost has moved from the origin to the waiters, whose latency is now the duration of a single computation. That is usually a large net win, because the computation is typically much more expensive than the wait and because the alternative is unbounded duplicate work. The risk is that the waiters have become dependent on one computation they did not perform and cannot influence. If that computation is slow, hangs, or is waiting on something that never returns, every waiter is stuck behind it even though most of them could have completed their own work. Three things keep that risk bounded and all three are required. The lock is per key, so an unrelated slow computation does not block anything else. The wait has a timeout, and a waiter that gives up is free to compute for itself rather than being held. And the value is written to the cache before the lock is released, so the waiters are waiting for a result that will exist rather than for work that is repeated on the next arrival. The second claims the miss disappears, which is false the first time and true only afterwards if the write succeeds. The third says the risk is absent because waiters time out, which ignores that a timed-out waiter still needs an answer. The last one confuses the lock with a longer cache lifetime.

questions.explanation: A pool is a promise about concurrency, and once the promises exceed the pool every additional request waits. The application asks for a connection, the pool has none free, and the request blocks in a queue inside the client library until either a connection comes back or the library's own wait limit expires. The symptom is therefore not that the database is unreachable. The database is healthy and is executing the thirty queries that are holding the connections, most of which are the slow ones. The service continues to accept requests, its own health check continues to pass, and the failures arrive as timeouts on requests that were never sent to the database. That combination is what makes this failure hard to attribute: the error says the database failed, the database's own monitoring says it is fine, and the application's monitoring says its error rate has risen. The useful signal is the pool's own queue depth and wait time, which are the earliest indication and the only ones that distinguish pool exhaustion from a slow database. The corrective design has three parts, and they address different things. A wait limit turns an unbounded wait into a bounded one. A much shorter limit on how long a query may run stops one slow statement from holding a connection at all, which is the measure that actually reduces the number of connections in use. And a per-caller cap on concurrent work stops one request stream from consuming the whole pool. The first distractor names the wrong component, and the symptom it describes is what a genuine connection failure looks like. The second assumes the pool grows, which defeats the point of having a fixed size. The last one confuses a per-request view with a per-process limit and misstates where the error is raised.

questions.explanation: The limit is enforced by the operating system against the process, and it is an allocation failure rather than a permission decision, so there is nothing to negotiate with it and nothing left to open. A service that reaches its cap cannot create a new file descriptor, which means it cannot accept a new connection, cannot open a new log file, cannot open the file it uses for its own health state, and cannot open a socket to a dependency. The reason this is worse than losing one request is that the descriptors that were left behind are usually the evidence. A process whose descriptors leak is the process that hit the cap, and the log file it was writing when it died is one of the things it can no longer open. The failure is also invisible from outside, because the process still answers on the descriptors it already holds: established connections keep working, so a health check that opens a new connection fails while every live request succeeds, and the two facts point in opposite directions. Two properties of the limit are worth knowing. It is typically inherited, so a process started from a parent inherits the parent's limit and cannot exceed it, which means raising it requires a change to the start of the process tree rather than to the application. And it is per process, so a service that forks workers has the limit applied to each of them independently. The defensible design is to set the cap high enough for the real working set, to count descriptors as a monitored quantity with an alert well before the cap, and to make sure the service can still write its own diagnostics when it is under pressure, which usually means reserving a small number of descriptors at startup. The second distractor gets the scope of the limit wrong, the third assumes a graceful failure path exists, and the last one treats a gradual leak as though it produced a gradual failure.

questions.explanation: The two numbers in the question are the whole diagnosis, because their difference is the growth rate of the backlog. Arrivals are 5000 a second and retirements are 1200 a second, so the queue gains 3800 entries every second and never shrinks. A thread pool with an unbounded queue has no mechanism that notices this. The workers are saturated, which looks healthy in every dashboard that reports worker utilisation, and the queue is a data structure in the same process that grows without limit. The service will therefore fail in one of three ways, and it will fail well after the operators stopped being worried: the queue's memory is exhausted and the process dies; the latency of every request grows in proportion to the queue length and callers time out first; or the queue's memory pressure triggers swapping and the whole process slows to a rate where even the retirement figure of 1200 a second is no longer achieved. The reason this is a denial-of-service property rather than a capacity property is that an attacker can create the divergence deliberately, and can create it with perfectly well-formed requests. Nothing about the traffic is invalid, so no filter will catch it, and the pool configuration that fails here is the default in most frameworks. The corrective design is to make the queue bounded and to decide in advance what happens at the bound. Rejecting is the usual choice for a request queue, because it puts a fast error in front of a slow one. Blocking is a different choice with a different cost, since it converts queue depth into thread occupancy. A pool with no queue at all, where a task that cannot start immediately is refused, is a third and is the most honest. The first distractor assumes a busy pool means the backlog is being worked off, which confuses activity with progress. The second says a full queue is reassuring, which is the opposite of what a growing queue means. The last one misreads the numbers and describes rate limiting that is not configured.
questions.hint: Subtract the completion rate from the arrival rate and ask what an unbounded structure does with the difference.

questions.explanation: The limit is a boundary, and the thing worth being precise about is what is on each side of it. Inside the boundary is one tenant's workload, which is stopped when it tries to exceed its share. Outside the boundary is everything else on the machine, which keeps its memory and keeps running. That is the whole achievement, and for a shared machine it is a large one: without the limit, one workload's allocation loop takes memory from every other workload until the operating system starts reclaiming pages indiscriminately, at which point the damage is no longer confined to the tenant that caused it. What the limit does not do is make the failure of that tenant clean. A process that exceeds its limit is typically terminated, and everything it was holding goes with it: open transactions, in-flight responses, work already done that was never committed, and any state that existed only in memory. The tenant experiences an interruption rather than an error, and if the workload was writing a file or emitting records, the interruption lands wherever the process happened to be. Two design points follow. First, a limit that terminates is much better than a limit that merely slows the workload, because a throttled allocation loop can be made to spin indefinitely while consuming the very resource it was throttled on. Second, a limit on a whole process is coarse, so a workload that leaks steadily rather than allocating in a burst will hit it slowly and be indistinguishable from a workload doing legitimate work. The first distractor assumes the allocation failure is detected and handled at the point of allocation, which is not how an enforced limit behaves. The third claims memory is returned immediately, which is true of a reclaiming system and not of an enforced one. The last one mistakes the granularity, and no per-request limit exists in this design at all.

questions.explanation: The resource being consumed is concurrency, not bandwidth, and that is what makes the technique cheap. A server that reads a request body as it arrives cannot do anything else with that connection until the body has been read, and reading is done by a worker. So a client that opens a connection, sends a few hundred bytes, and then stops is holding one worker and one buffer for as long as it cares to hold them, while contributing almost nothing to the arrival rate the operator is watching. The cost is proportional to the number of slow connections, not to the volume they carry, which is why traffic dashboards do not show it: the bytes-per-second figure stays low and flat while the connection count and the worker utilisation climb. That combination is the signature, and it is worth being able to recognise it. A second variant achieves the same thing with almost no data at all by opening a connection and sending nothing, which defeats any body limit while consuming the same worker. What follows from this is that the defences have to be about time and concurrency rather than about size. A limit on the body size bounds what a legitimate request can cost but does nothing about a small slow one. A read timeout, short by the standards of a large upload and generous by the standards of an interactive request, bounds how long any one connection may occupy a worker. A limit on concurrent connections per source bounds how many workers one host can hold. A limit on the time a worker may spend on a single request bounds the cost even when the client is well behaved and simply slow on a bad network. All four are needed, because each addresses a different way of holding a worker. The first distractor assumes an idle connection is free, which is the belief that makes this technique work. The third confuses worker time with reserved link capacity. The last one describes a different defect, in which the server buffers a whole body, and buffering is not what reading incrementally does.

questions.explanation: The growth is combinatorial, not linear, and that is the entire point. A pattern made of two adjacent groups that can each take a variable number of characters matches a string in many different ways, and an engine that has to prove that none of them matches is obliged to try them in turn before it can report failure. If the first group must take at least one character, the number of ways to split a string of length n into a first part and a second part is the number of ways to choose where the first part ends, which is n minus one. Nest that structure and the count multiplies rather than adds, so the work needed to reject a non-matching input grows exponentially with the length. A forty-character input is therefore not forty units of work; it is on the order of a hundred billion candidate divisions, and at any plausible rate of trial that is seconds of processor time on a request that is a few dozen bytes long. Three properties make this unusually bad as a denial of service. The input is small, so no size limit catches it. The input is well formed, so no validation rejects it. And the failure is in the validator, which by construction runs before the work it is protecting, so the expensive component is on the critical path of every request. That last point is what distinguishes this from an expensive computation the attacker has to supply a lot of data for. The first distractor assumes the engine abandons a branch at the first mismatch, which is exactly the behaviour that does not occur: a mismatch inside a quantified group is a reason to try a different split, not to give up. The third confuses input length with search space. The last one is a linear argument, and the growth it describes is the one thing this class of pattern does not have.

questions.explanation: The cheapest thing that works is a bound on how long the engine is permitted to spend, because it attacks the quantity that is actually unbounded. Anchoring, rewriting the pattern, and adding hardware all leave the search space exactly as it was; they change where the engine starts or how much work each trial costs, and a search that is exponential stays exponential. questions.explanation: A timeout on the caller and a cancellation of the work are different things, and almost every system has the first without the second. The application's five-second limit applies to how long it will wait for a result, so after five seconds the request handler returns an error to its caller and the thread becomes free. Nothing in that sequence reaches into the database and stops the statement, so the statement continues, and it continues holding whatever it holds. If the statement has modified rows, it holds locks on them until it commits or rolls back, and until then every other statement that needs the same rows is queued behind it. Those queued statements are not queued politely either: they occupy the application's own workers, so each of them burns its five seconds too, fails, and is retried, and the retries join the queue. The result is that one abandoned report becomes an application-wide outage whose symptom is a rising timeout rate and nothing else. Two things make it worse and both are common. The report is often read-only, so nobody thinks of it as a writer, while its query planner has chosen a plan that does write to temporary structures and does acquire locks it will hold for the duration. And the timeout values are chosen from the latency of normal requests, so they are far too generous to bound a query that was never going to finish. The defences that work are a server-side limit on the statement's own runtime, which stops it where the work actually is, and a limit on how long a transaction may hold locks, which bounds the damage one statement can do. The second distractor assumes the caller's timeout cancels the work, which is the belief that produces this incident. The third assumes readers are harmless to writers, which is false for both locks and temporary structures. The last one misapplies the timeout to the queued writers rather than to the statement holding them.

questions.explanation: The shape of the two measurements is the finding, and the shape is more informative than either number. Throughput rose by 5 per cent when concurrency doubled, which means the second cohort of callers was not doing twice the work; it was waiting. The response time did not rise in proportion either: it went from 40 ms at the 99th percentile to 900 ms, more than twenty times, while the arrival rate barely moved. Both of those are signatures of a shared resource that is now serialising the requests, and the standard explanation is that the extra time is queueing rather than processing. That distinction matters because the two causes have opposite remedies. If the cost per request had genuinely doubled, the answer is more capacity, and the linear relationship between concurrency and cost would show it. If the cost per request is unchanged and the added time is waiting, more capacity delays the problem and does not remove it, because the contention is a property of the design rather than of the machine. The practical way to tell them apart is to hold the arrival rate constant and vary the concurrency: with a fixed arrival rate, added concurrency should not change the response time at all, and if it does, something is serialising. Once the contention is identified, the fixes are structural. Reducing the time each request holds the contended resource, which is the highest-leverage change and is usually a matter of shortening a transaction. Reducing the number of distinct resources requests need at the same time, so the contention points are fewer and hotter and can be managed. Or accepting lower throughput per worker and raising the worker count, which trades memory for concurrency and is a real answer when the contention is coarse. The first distractor assumes a constant per-request cost and draws the opposite conclusion. The second dismisses the measurement without saying what would make it believable. The last one asserts a relationship that does not hold and then explains away the data that contradicts it.
questions.hint: Compare the change in throughput with the change in response time, and ask where the extra time is spent.
questions.learningObjective: read a concurrency measurement as evidence of contention rather than of capacity

questions.explanation: A check that confirms a port is listening establishes exactly one thing: that something has bound that port and has not closed it. It says nothing about whether the process behind the port has any capacity, whether its outbound dependencies are reachable, whether its work queue is empty, or whether it can complete the specific request the load balancer is about to send it. Every one of those can be false while the port remains open, and each of them produces the same outcome: the instance stays in rotation, the load balancer keeps sending it work, and the work sits in a queue that nothing is draining. The reason this configuration is so common is that it is the one that never takes the instance out of service for a reason unrelated to the instance. A check that depends on a downstream store will remove every instance simultaneously during a downstream outage, which is worse than useless if any of them could still serve a cached or degraded response. A check that depends on a dependency the instance does not need will do the same. So the design question is not whether the check should be richer, it is which failure should take the instance out. In practice there are two answers and they are used together. A cheap check on whether the process can serve at all, run often, catches the instance that is wedged. A check on whether this instance can serve the requests it is about to receive, run less often, catches the instance that is alive but not useful, and it is the one that has to be specific enough to distinguish useful from not useful. Neither of them is the port check, and the port check is worth keeping only as the coarsest of the three. questions.explanation: The release of a resource has to happen on every path out of the code that acquires it, and this function has four ways out and releases on two of them. questions.explanation: The outer plus is applied to something that can already match a variable number of characters, and that is the structural cause. The group in the middle can match one or more occurrences of a, and the outer plus says one or more of those groups. A run of n characters can be divided into a sequence of non-empty runs in 2^(n-1) different ways, and the engine has to try each one before it can conclude that no division is followed by the required final character. For the thirty characters in the input that is 2^29, or 536870912, candidate divisions, and the trailing x guarantees that every one of them fails. At any plausible rate of trial, that is seconds of processor time inside a function whose input is thirty-one characters long. What makes it a denial of service rather than a slow function is the ratio between the two sizes. The attacker spends 31 bytes and acquires a worker for as long as the trial takes, and the worker is doing nothing else, so the number of concurrent attackers needed to occupy a service is small. It is also worth noticing that the trailing x is not doing anything clever: the input is a valid, ordinary string, and the only reason it is expensive is the shape of the pattern. The same effect appears in any pattern where a quantified group contains another quantifier that can accept the same characters, and the general rule is that such a pattern is worth rewriting even when no attacker has been observed using it. The three defences are complementary and each is worth having: rewrite the pattern so that the nesting is gone, bound the work the matcher may do so a future pattern cannot reintroduce the problem, and validate the field with something that is not a pattern at all where that is practical. The other three options each describe a property the pattern does not have, and the engine is not optimising any of them away because it cannot know in advance which division will succeed.

questions.explanation: Four of the settings in that configuration are the default, and each of the four corresponds to a resource a client can spend without sending much traffic. There is no limit on the body, so the memory the edge must hold for a request in progress is bounded by the largest body the client claims to be sending rather than by anything the operator chose. Before it, every caller that arrived during the recomputation started its own, so the origin saw one expensive operation per caller and the duration of the spike was the duration of one computation multiplied by the number of callers. questions.explanation: A scrubbing service sits in front of the workload's own capacity and decides what to let through, which is the one place in the architecture where the incoming volume can be reduced rather than merely survived. That is a genuine advantage over every control the workload itself can apply, because a workload cannot refuse traffic before it has arrived and paid for the bandwidth. The price is a change in what the workload is responsible for, and that is the part teams get wrong. Everything the scrubbing service forwards is now traffic the workload must handle, and forwarding is a decision somebody else made: a policy that is too permissive forwards the flood along with the good traffic, and a policy that is too aggressive forwards a fraction of the legitimate requests as well. So the workload's own limits do not become unnecessary, they become the last line rather than the only one, and they have to be configured with the expectation that a fraction of what arrives is unwanted. Two further properties follow from putting a third party on the data path. The scrubbing service sees the traffic, so anything sensitive in it is now visible to that operator, and the workload's own address is no longer the only way to reach it if the scrubbing service can be bypassed. And the dependency is now a single point whose failure removes the workload entirely, so there has to be a decision about what happens when it does: fail closed and take the service down, or fail open and expose the workload to whatever arrives. The second is the availability-first choice and it is a real decision with a real cost. The first option names both halves correctly. The other three each claim a completeness the arrangement does not have, and the last one claims it is free.
questions.hint: Ask where the unwanted traffic is stopped, and what the workload still has to handle.
questions.learningObjective: state what a scrubbing service changes about where unwanted traffic is stopped and what it leaves the workload owning

options.text: It removes unwanted traffic before it reaches the workload's own capacity, and the workload still owns everything the scrubbing service forwards, including what a permissive policy lets through

options.misconception: claims the arrangement is unconditional
options.text: It removes the workload's need for its own limits entirely, since the scrubbing service decides what arrives and the workload can no longer be given more work than it can accept

options.misconception: treats the change as free of any new exposure
options.text: It shifts the risk rather than reducing it, because the third party now sees all of the traffic and a failure of the third party removes the workload as surely as the flood would have

options.misconception: denies the workload any residual responsibility
options.text: It hands the workload nothing, because traffic that has passed the scrubbing service is by definition legitimate and the workload is right to treat all of it as work it must accept

questions.explanation: The order is set by one asymmetry: confirming the signal is quick and reversible, and everything after it is neither. A single metric can be misleading in a way that matters here, because a service under load can report a healthy error rate for a while and a saturated one can report a healthy response time, so the first action is to corroborate the signal against at least two others that should have moved together. Once the signal is established, the next step is to stop the failure propagating, because containment is what protects the users who are not involved in the incident and it is also what stops the evidence from being destroyed by further change. Diagnosis comes third, and putting it second is the common mistake: a cause established by changing things is a cause established under conditions nobody will ever see again, and the change that helped becomes indistinguishable from the change that hurt. The record comes last for a reason that is easy to state and easy to skip. It is not documentation for its own sake; it is the only thing that makes the next occurrence comparable to this one, and the person who writes it cannot write it afterwards from memory, because by then the detail that mattered has been reconstructed from logs nobody kept. Two properties of a good order are worth naming. Nothing in it depends on a conclusion that has not been established, and nothing in it destroys state that the next step needs. Done in a different order, either the diagnosis is contaminated by the containment or the record is written by someone who has already forgotten which of four changes was made first.
questions.hint: Ask which steps are reversible and which change the system you are diagnosing.

Record what was changed and what the symptom was, so the next occurrence can be compared against this one rather than reasoned about from memory
Establish why the service saturated, since a control applied without the cause is a guess that the next change to the workload will quietly remove

questions.explanation: The threshold comes first because it is the decision everything else depends on and because choosing it wrongly makes the other three pointless. A threshold set at the point where the service is already saturated acts after the damage, since by then the queue is long, the workers are pinned and the latency is already the thing the load was supposed to avoid. A threshold set from the measured service rate, with a margin, acts while the system is still able to answer and while there is still something to protect. Deciding what to shed comes second, and it is a decision rather than a default because shedding by arrival order sheds the expensive long-running requests alongside the cheap ones, which can be worse than no shedding at all: the service stops accepting the work that would have finished the jobs its other work depends on. Protecting the cheap and short requests and shedding the long ones keeps the service looking and behaving like a service, which matters for the users who did nothing to cause the problem. The refusal has to be made actionable third, because a refusal the caller cannot interpret is a refusal the caller retries, and the retries arrive at a service that is already shedding. A distinct status, and a signal the caller can act on, are what convert the shed from a loop into a working arrangement. The observation comes last because the shed's effect cannot be judged until it is running, and the specific thing to watch is what happened to the work that was kept. A shed that removes the work the service needed in order to finish other work has not shed load, it has changed the shape of the failure, and the only way to know is to look at the completed work rather than at the refused requests.
questions.hint: Ask which decision the other three depend on, and what the refusal has to be to the caller.
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of shedding load without making the failure worse

options.text: Decide which classes of request to shed and which to protect, since shedding by arrival order discards expensive long-running work along with cheap work
Make the refusal distinguishable to the caller, with a status and a signal that the caller should not retry immediately into a service that is shedding
Set the shed threshold from the measured service rate rather than a round number, so the service sheds before it is saturated rather than afterwards
Watch what happened to the requests that were kept, since a shed that removes the work needed to finish other work has changed the failure rather than reduced it

questions.explanation: The order follows the structure of the defect rather than the structure of the fix. The existing loop amplifies every error equally, so the first question is which errors it is amplifying, because a policy that bounds the retries of an error a retry cannot fix is still an amplifier with a smaller rate. That question has to be answered before the numbers are chosen, since the cap and the pause only make sense once the population of retryable failures is known. The bound and the growth come next, and they are the two halves of the load reduction: the cap limits the total load one caller adds over the life of an outage, and the growing pause limits the rate at which it is added during it. Neither alone is sufficient, because a cap of ten with no pause produces ten simultaneous retries per caller and a pause with no cap produces an unbounded number spread thinly over an unbounded time. The random component comes third because it addresses a different failure from the first two. A cap and a pause make each caller well behaved, and thousands of well-behaved callers all failing at the same instant are still a synchronised spike, so the random component is what makes the aggregate arrival rate smooth rather than peaky. The observation comes last, and it is not a formality. A retry policy is a per-client property and the damage is an aggregate property, so a fleet of clients each inside its own cap can still be a sustained flood, and the only place that shows up is the dependency's own arrival rate and the caller's own success rate over time. Watching those two together is what tells you the cap is set correctly rather than merely present. Done in another order, either the policy is tuned for the wrong errors or the fleet's behaviour is never measured at all.
questions.hint: Ask which errors should be retried at all, then which property bounds total load, which bounds the rate, and which smooths the fleet.

options.text: Separate the errors worth retrying from those that are not, so the loop stops amplifying the failures that no retry can resolve
Add a cap on the number of attempts and a pause that grows with each one, bounding both the total load one caller adds and the rate at which it is added
Add a random component to the pause, so callers that failed at the same instant do not retry at the same instant and meet the recovery as one spike
Observe the aggregate retry rate against the dependency, since a fleet of clients each inside its own cap can still be a sustained flood

questions.explanation: The breaker is three decisions and a measurement, and the two decisions about behaviour come before the one about consequences. The condition comes first because it is what determines how often everything else happens. A rate over a window handles both the sudden total failure and the steady partial one, which is the case that catches teams out, whereas a count of consecutive failures is reset by every success and therefore never fires for a dependency that is failing one request in five. Setting it from measured behaviour rather than from a round number matters for the same reason: too low and the breaker opens during ordinary variation and becomes an outage amplifier, too high and it opens after the damage. The trial state comes second, and its absence is what makes a breaker a one-way door. A breaker that only opens is a switch that has to be reset by a person, which converts a transient dependency problem into a deployment at three in the morning. The rule for the trial, how many calls are admitted, what proportion has to succeed, and how long the answer lasts, is what makes recovery automatic and bounded at the same time. The consequence decision comes third because it is the one with a user-visible effect and it has to be made before the breaker first opens rather than during the incident. Whether a saved response is served instead of an error is a real decision: it is the difference between a degraded service and a broken one, and it comes with the obligation to label the answer as old. The measurement comes last, and the specific thing to watch is the dependency's own arrival rate, because a breaker reduces it and that change is visible on the other side. A caller whose error rate improves while the breaker is open has learned nothing about the dependency.
questions.hint: Ask which decision determines how often the rest happens, and which one makes recovery automatic.

options.text: Decide what the breaker does while it is open, including whether a saved response can be served and whether the answer is labelled as stale

Add the trial state and the rule for closing and reopening it, since a breaker that only opens is a switch somebody has to reset by hand
Watch the dependency's own arrival rate, because the breaker reduces this caller's load on it and that change is visible from the other side

questions.explanation: The order is set by two asymmetries: what can be lost and what can be undone. Verifying the data comes first because a cutover to a region that does not hold the current data is not a partial failure, it is a loss, and no amount of care in the later steps recovers writes that were never replicated. The decision about simultaneous writes comes second and is the one that is easiest to skip and worst to skip. During a cutover both regions can accept traffic for a period, and if they both accept writes the two orders diverge, at which point reconciling them is a data engineering project rather than an operational one. Deciding in advance that one region is authoritative for writes during the move, and that the other will not accept them, is what keeps the cutover a routing change rather than a fork. Moving read traffic first is the third step and it is the one that makes the cutover observable at a size that can be reversed: read errors and stale reads show up quickly, they are attributable, and rolling them back costs nothing. Write traffic is last because a write that lands in the new region and cannot then be read is an outage, whereas a read that is slow is an inconvenience. Each step also has a defined exit condition, and the exit conditions are what stop a cutover becoming a sequence of hopeful advances. The first option names both halves, the second proposes starting with the irreversible step, the third leaves the data question until after the traffic has moved, and the last one skips the data check entirely and so can lose writes that the second region never received.
questions.hint: Ask what can be lost and what can be undone, and put the irreversible step after the reversible one.

Move a share of read traffic first and watch the result, so that a mistake is visible at a size that can be reversed without a data problem
Decide which region accepts writes during the move, because a period in which both accept them forks the order and reconciling two orders is not an operation
Move write traffic only after reads are healthy in the new region, since a write that lands where it cannot be read is an outage rather than a migration

questions.explanation: Every step after the first is about not making the restart worse than the reason for it, and that is what fixes the order. Marking the instance as not ready and stopping new work comes first because it is the only step that reduces the work in flight, and everything after it is easier when the set of things that have to finish is known and no longer growing. Bringing the replacement into rotation before the old instance exits comes second, and it is the step that prevents a capacity dip: a rolling restart that removes an instance before its replacement is serving converts a routine deployment into an availability event, and it does so at exactly the moment when the remaining instances are carrying the full load. Waiting for in-flight work comes third, bounded, because unbounded waiting is the failure mode of a graceful shutdown. A request waiting on a dependency that never answers will otherwise hold the instance open indefinitely, and a deployment that blocks on a stuck request is a deployment that has turned a small problem into a slow one and possibly a manual intervention. Exiting after the bound is correct even though it loses the work that did not finish, because the alternative is an instance that does not go away at all. The observation comes last, and the thing to watch is the response time and error rate on the remaining instances during the redistribution, because a restart that removes capacity during a period of high demand moves the failure rather than removing it. A restart completed successfully is not a restart that was safe; it is a restart that finished, and those are different claims.
questions.hint: Ask which step reduces the work in flight, and which step prevents capacity from dipping during the replacement.
questions.learningObjective: order the steps of a graceful restart under sustained load

options.text: Mark the instance as not ready and stop accepting new work, so the load balancer stops selecting it and the set of outstanding requests stops growing
Confirm the replacement instance is in rotation and answering before the old one exits, so capacity never dips below what the current load requires
Wait for in-flight work to finish within a bounded period and then exit regardless, so a stuck request cannot hold a deployment open indefinitely
Watch the remaining instances as the load is redistributed, since a restart that removes capacity during a busy period has moved the failure rather than removed it

questions.explanation: A is the only measurement that describes the service consuming its own capacity and nothing else, and the arithmetic in the other three is what rules them out. In A the arrival rate is 40 times normal and every request returns 200, which means the service parsed, processed and answered all of them, and the only thing that can be true is that it did so by using the time other users needed. That is exhaustion with no error anywhere, which is the shape of the whole class of incident this unit is about. B is a large number that does not bite: 20000 half-finished connections fit inside a table that holds 50000, so the table is partly full rather than exhausted, and a partly full table is not a failure. C looks alarming and is not: 30 requests a second each occupying a worker for 40 milliseconds is 1.2 concurrent validations, which is a rounding error against any service worth measuring. D describes a night in which the incident happened somewhere else, since the edge refused nine requests in ten and the service never saw them; that is a good outcome for the service and a statement about the edge's policy, not about anything the service suffered. The value of ranking them this way is that each number points somewhere different, and a responder who has only a dashboard full of such figures has to know which resource each one belongs to before deciding where to look. The first option does that. The second picks the largest number, which is a heuristic that fails whenever the largest number is not the one that mattered. The third and fourth each promote a measurement that the arithmetic or the topology makes harmless.
questions.hint: Ask which measurement describes the service itself consuming capacity with no error, and check the arithmetic in the others.

questions.explanation: A capacity claim is a statement about a rate, and only one of these reports is a measurement at a stated rate held for long enough to be meaningful. B does the two things that matter. It holds the load constant, so the figure describes one operating point rather than an average over a ramp, and it holds it for long enough that anything with a slow failure, a leak, a cache that fills or a queue that grows has had time to show up. A 99th percentile rather than a mean is the other half, because a mean over a held load is a statement about the typical request while the resource that runs out is exhausted by a tail. The other three each fail in a way worth being able to name. C's average of 40 ms and its 99th percentile of 4 s are not in conflict, they are the same data summarised two ways, and the gap between them is the finding: a small fraction of requests are taking a hundred times the typical time, which is a queue, a lock, or a slow dependency, and it is invisible in the figure most dashboards lead with. D measured a tenth of the production peak, so it is a true statement about a load the service will never see, and it is the standard way a capacity report ends up being quoted for a claim it does not support. A's ramp is the interesting one, because a ramp is the only way to find the failure point and the average reported from it is the least useful number it produces: the mean over a ramp that ends in failure is dominated by the fast part and says nothing about the last ten per cent. The right question to ask of A is what the 99th percentile was at the point the ramp stopped. The first option leads with the mean, the third leads with the figure that is contradicted by its own tail, and the last one treats a test at a tenth of the real load as a capacity statement.
questions.hint: Ask which report states a rate, holds it, and summarises the tail rather than the average.

questions.explanation: All four tests report the same number, and the number is meaningless without knowing how the load was offered and whether the generator could offer it. C is the only one where the arrival schedule was independent of the service's replies and the generator still had most of its capacity unused, so the 90 per cent on the service is a real measurement of the service reaching its own limit. Everything about that combination matters. A fixed schedule means the offered rate does not fall when the service slows, which is what production does and what a closed loop cannot reproduce. A generator that is not itself saturated means the figure is not a statement about the test rig. A service at 90 per cent means the test is close to the interesting part of the curve rather than comfortably below it. The other three each measure something else. A and B both have the generator at 90 per cent or above, so the limiting factor was the machine sending the requests, and the service's low own-CPU figure is exactly what you would expect when the client is the constraint: the reported throughput is the generator's maximum, not the service's. D removes that problem by using a closed loop with a fast generator, and then leaves a different one, because 400 users sending as fast as replies arrive is a self-limiting offered rate, so the test establishes the service's behaviour at whatever rate 400 users can sustain and nothing about what happens above it. The other mistake the closed-loop tests share is that they cannot see the queue at all: a client that waits for a reply before sending the next request reduces its own arrival rate as the service slows, so the service never sees the load that would have caused the failure it is being tested for. The first option leads with the generator figures, the second with a rate nobody offered, and the last one picks the test whose own load was lowest.
