questions.explanation: The four configurations differ in what they do to the dependency and what they do to the caller, and only one of them bounds both. C bounds the load the caller adds, because five attempts is a hard stop and the growing pause means the attempts are not simultaneous, and it bounds what the caller waits for, because after five attempts it gets a saved response or an error rather than a fifth of the dependency's downtime multiplied by its own pause schedule. The saved response is a real design decision and has to be labelled, since a caller acting on a response that is twenty minutes old needs to know that. A is defensible for a call that is cheap and non-idempotent, where a retry is worse than a failure, and indefensible for anything expensive, because it gives up on the first sign of trouble and reports a dependency problem as a total outage of that one function. B is the worst of the four and it is the default in a great many client libraries: it removes the caller's own failure but multiplies the dependency's load at precisely the moment the dependency has least capacity for it, and the multiplication is by the number of callers rather than by one. D is the configuration that produces the queue everybody is trying to avoid, since every caller waits for the full duration and then succeeds, which means the number of callers held open is a function of the outage rather than of anything the service chose. The useful habit is to ask of any such policy which quantity it bounds on each side, and to notice that C is the only one that bounds both. The other three each name a mechanism that is real and describe it as if it were sufficient.

answer.exemplar: A mean is a statement about the average request and almost nobody's experience is the average request. The arithmetic is simple and it is why the two facts can both be true. Suppose 97 per cent of requests are answered in 30 ms and 3 per cent take 13 seconds. The mean is close to 420 ms, which already sounds bad, and if the slow fraction is 1 per cent and the slow requests take 4 seconds the mean is 70 ms, which sounds fine. Either way the figure moves with the fraction of slow requests and hardly at all with how slow they are, so it can stay acceptable while the users having a bad time are having an extremely bad time. The people who complain are the ones in the slow fraction, and their experience is bounded by the slow figure rather than by the mean. Worse, the slow fraction is usually not random. It tends to be the requests that are large, that touch the contended resource, that arrive when the service is busiest, or that belong to one client on one region, so the population complaining is a specific population rather than a random sample of the whole. That is why an average can sit at 40 ms for a week while a named customer reports that the service is unusable. The second reason the dashboard is unhelpful is that the mean is not stable under load. As a service approaches saturation, the mean rises smoothly and slowly, because the slow requests are still a small fraction of the total for a long time, and by the time the mean doubles the tail is already minutes long. A mean is therefore a poor early warning as well as a poor description. What the service should report is a distribution rather than a summary: the 50th, 95th and 99th percentiles, each stated with the rate they were measured at, plus the count of requests above a threshold that the callers actually care about, plus the error rate counted against the number of requests accepted rather than the number completed. The percentiles have to be computed over a window and shown as a time series, because a percentile that is stable for an hour and then jumps is a different incident from one that drifts. And the threshold count is the figure that maps onto a complaint, since it answers how many people are having a bad time rather than how long the average one took.

questions.explanation: Because a mean is a property of the distribution's centre and the people who complain are not at its centre. The mean moves with the fraction of slow requests and barely at all with how slow those requests are, so it can hold at 40 ms while a small population is waiting many seconds, and it can stay near that figure right through the period in which the service is approaching saturation and the slow fraction is still small. The mean is also a poor early warning for the same reason: it rises smoothly and late, whereas the tail rises early and sharply, so a service watched on its average is being warned about a problem that is already well advanced. What belongs on the dashboard instead is a distribution, and the specific figures that matter are the percentiles at a stated rate together with a count of requests above the latency the callers actually care about. That count is the one that maps onto a complaint, because a complaint is a person, not a percentile. It also helps to remember that the slow fraction is usually not a random sample: it tends to be the large requests, the contended ones, the busiest periods, and sometimes one client on one region, so the population suffering is identifiable and the average says nothing about it. Reporting the percentiles without the rate they were measured at repeats the original mistake in a different place, since a percentile at 5 per cent of capacity and at 95 per cent are not the same claim. The other errors are worth naming: treating the mean as a description of what users experience, treating it as an early warning, and treating it as a figure that can be compared between services whose work differs.
questions.hint: Ask what a mean is a statement about, and which users are not at the mean.

answer.exemplar: Adding instances multiplies the arrival rate and leaves the exhausted resource alone, so under a shared bottleneck the attempt makes things worse rather than neutral. Saturation means that one specific resource has run out, and the useful question is which one. If it is internal to each instance, then adding instances is exactly the right response and the service should return to normal. If it is shared, then it is not: a database connection limit, a table lock, a single-threaded dependency, a queue whose consumer count is fixed, an upstream that answers at a bounded rate, or the bandwidth of the link the instances share. In every one of those cases the added instances do not add capacity, they add arrivals to a resource that was already at its limit, and contention rises. The second-order effects are what make the incident worse rather than merely unchanged. Each new instance holds its own connections, so the pool is drained faster. Each new instance retries, so the arrival rate at the shared resource is higher than the arrival rate at the service. Each new instance caches cold, so the expensive path runs on all of them at once. And the operational cost is real: ten more instances is ten more things to be restarted, patched and paid for, during an incident, by people who should be diagnosing something. The check to do first is the utilisation of the shared resource itself rather than of the instances, and the diagnostic that settles it is deliberately simple. If the shared resource's utilisation is already at its ceiling, the instances are not the constraint. If each instance is individually at its ceiling and the shared resource has headroom, the instances were the constraint and the scale-out was correct. If neither is at a ceiling and the service is still slow, the resource is somewhere the dashboard does not cover, and the queue depth is where to look. The other mistake worth naming is scaling on the symptom rather than on the measurement: a service that is slow because a downstream is slow will appear to improve when the added instances time out faster and produce errors, which is a worse outcome dressed as progress.

questions.explanation: Because the instances and the exhausted resource are usually not the same thing, and scaling out multiplies the pressure on the second while doing nothing for the first. Saturation has a cause, and the cause is a specific resource at a specific limit. When that resource lives inside the instance, more instances is the correct and complete answer. When it is shared, the attempt is not merely ineffective: each added instance brings its own connections, its own retries and its own cold cache, so the arrival rate at the shared resource rises while the rate at which it can serve work stays fixed, and the contention gets worse. The classic shared cases are a connection limit on the store, a lock held by one long statement, a dependency that is single-threaded or that answers at a bounded rate, a consumer group whose consumer count is fixed, and the bandwidth of the link the instances share. The first thing to check is the shared resource's own utilisation rather than the instances', and the test is simple: if the shared resource is already at its ceiling the instances are not the constraint, and if every instance is individually at its ceiling while the shared resource has headroom then they were. If neither is at a ceiling, the constrained resource is somewhere the dashboard does not reach, and queue depth is the place to look, since a queue that is deep while every component looks idle means the wait is somewhere downstream of where you are looking. There is also a sequencing point: scaling is a decision that costs money and takes time to reverse, and taking it during an incident without the measurement converts a bounded problem into an unbounded one. The specific mistake to avoid is reading an improvement in latency after the scale-out as the fix working, because a service that is timing out faster and returning errors will look faster and be less available. The three distractors each describe a real mechanism and treat it as decisive on its own.
questions.hint: Ask whether the exhausted resource is inside the instance or shared by all of them.
questions.learningObjective: explain why adding instances can fail to relieve saturation and what to check first

answer.exemplar: A closed-loop generator makes the offered rate a function of the service's own speed, so the test quietly stops asking the question it appears to ask. The mechanism is one line of logic. Each virtual user sends a request, waits for the reply, and only then sends the next one, so the rate at which the generator offers load is the number of users divided by the response time. When the service slows down, each user waits longer, and the offered rate falls in exactly the same proportion. The service therefore never sees the load that would have broken it, and the test reports a throughput figure at which the service was responding comfortably because the load was withdrawn the moment the response time rose. Production is the opposite. Real users are not a closed loop: a person does not stop clicking when the page is slow, an automated caller with a fixed schedule keeps sending, and a fleet of clients with retries sends more than it did before. So the failure the closed-loop test is supposed to find is the one failure it is structurally unable to produce, and a passing result means the generator's own arithmetic held rather than that the service was safe. The second problem compounds the first. Because the offered rate falls as latency rises, the test cannot measure latency at a fixed rate either: any figure it produces is a point on a curve the generator itself drew, and the only way to ask what the service does at 5000 requests a second is to offer 5000 requests a second. The alternative is an open-loop generator that sends on a schedule chosen in advance and does not slow down when the service does. It has its own difficulties, and they are worth knowing rather than dismissing. If the offered rate exceeds what the service can retire, the difference accumulates in the generator's own backlog, so the generator needs enough capacity to keep the schedule for the length of the test and the measured latency has to be attributed to a send time rather than to a wait for a free slot. That is the coordinated-omission problem, and it is the price of asking the right question. The honest summary is that a closed loop measures the service under a load it has already adapted to, which is a useful measurement of something and is not a capacity test.

questions.explanation: Because the offered load becomes a function of the thing being measured, so the test withdraws the load exactly when the service needs it most. With one request per virtual user outstanding, the offered rate is the number of users divided by the response time, so a service that slows to a tenth of its speed is offered a tenth of the load and never experiences the arrival rate that would have taken it down. Production does not behave that way: a fixed-schedule caller keeps sending, a person keeps clicking, and a fleet with retries sends more than it did before the slowdown. So the failure the test is meant to find is the one failure its own logic prevents, and a passing result is a statement about the generator's arithmetic rather than about the service. The second consequence is that the test cannot state a latency at a rate, because any figure it produces is a point on a curve the generator drew rather than a measurement at a chosen load. What should generate the load instead is an open-loop generator that sends on a schedule fixed in advance and does not slow down when the service does. That has its own difficulty, and it is worth naming rather than waving away: when the offered rate exceeds what the service retires, the difference accumulates as a backlog in the generator, and if the generator is not large enough to hold the schedule the measured latency is contaminated by the generator's own queue rather than by the service's. The fix for that is to make the generator large enough for the duration of the test and to timestamp each request when it was scheduled, so the latency is measured from the intended send time and the missing interval is visible instead of invisible. That is the coordinated-omission problem, and it is the price of asking the right question. The other two errors are worth distinguishing from this one: measuring the average rather than the tail, and running the test on hardware that is not the hardware the service will run on.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the offered rate when the service slows down.
questions.learningObjective: explain why a closed-loop load test understates production and what should generate the load

answer.exemplar: A dashboard is a summary over a chosen population, and an availability figure computed over requests that completed successfully will be green for as long as the failures are of a kind that never became a completed request. There are several ways this happens and they are worth separating, because each has a different fix. The first is the denominator. If the figure is the proportion of completed requests that succeeded, then a request that is queued, times out, is refused at the edge, or is never accepted does not appear in it at all, and a service in which two thirds of its callers receive a fast error has a perfect success rate. The count of requests that were accepted and then failed is a different number and is the one users experience. The second is aggregation across instances. Availability is often reported as the mean across instances, and a mean is 100 per cent whenever the one instance in four that is broken is diluted by three that are fine, so the dashboard reads green while a quarter of the traffic is failing. The same happens across regions and across services when a dependency's failures are reported only from the caller that noticed. The third is the choice of denominator interval. A five-minute window smooths a one-minute outage to two per cent and a rolling weekly figure smooths a bad day to a number that does not move, and both are legitimate arithmetic applied to a question nobody asked. The fourth is that the probe used for the health check answers a question the incident does not involve: the port is open, the process is alive, and the instance is still in rotation being sent the work it cannot do. The fifth is the definition of the success. A 200 returned from a degraded response, from a cache holding stale data, or from a fallback path counts as a success in every standard metric while being a failure to the caller. What makes this visible is a set of measures chosen to be hard to satisfy accidentally. The ratio of accepted to completed connections, which falls when work is being refused. Queue depth per instance rather than in aggregate, which shows the one that is broken. The error rate counted against arrivals rather than completions. Latency percentiles per instance and per region, so a localised failure is not averaged away. The count of callers receiving a fast failure, which is the figure a complaint is actually about. And an alert whose condition is stated in terms of user-visible behaviour rather than in terms of process state, because a process is rarely the thing that is broken.

questions.explanation: Because an availability figure is a summary over a population, and several different populations all look healthy while a third of the callers are failing. The most common one is the denominator: a success rate computed over completed requests excludes everything that never completed, so requests that are queued, timed out, refused at the edge or never accepted are invisible and a service returning fast errors to most of its callers scores perfectly. The second is aggregation, because availability reported as a mean across instances is 100 per cent whenever the broken instance is diluted by the healthy ones, and the same arithmetic hides a failure confined to one region or to one caller. The third is the window, since a five-minute or weekly average is a legitimate number applied to a question nobody asked and it smooths exactly the events worth noticing. The fourth is the probe, since a health check that asks whether the process is alive keeps an instance in rotation that is already unable to do the work being sent to it. The fifth is the definition of success, since a 200 from a stale cache, a degraded response or a fallback path is a success to every metric and a failure to the caller. The measures that expose all five are chosen to be hard to satisfy accidentally: accepted against completed connections, queue depth per instance rather than in aggregate, error rate counted against arrivals, latency percentiles broken out by instance and region, and a count of callers receiving a fast failure, which is the number a complaint is actually about. The important structural point is that an alert should be written in terms of what the caller experiences, because a process is rarely the thing that is broken. The distractors each pick one of these mechanisms and treat it as the whole explanation, and each is a real mechanism, so the item is asking which one is doing the work in this particular dashboard.
questions.hint: Ask what population the figure is computed over, and what happens to requests that never complete.

questions.explanation: Three conversions have to be done in the right order and each one is a place to go wrong by a factor. A bit is not a byte, so 10^9 bits a second is 10^9 divided by 8, which is 125000000 bytes a second on the wire. That figure is what has to arrive, because the bottleneck is the target's inbound link rather than anything behind it, and a filter that discards packets after they have arrived does not reduce the arriving volume. The amplification factor of 50 is a ratio of response bytes to request bytes, so each byte the attacker sends brings 50 bytes of response, and the required request rate is therefore 125000000 divided by 50, which is 2500000 bytes a second. The same answer can be reached in the other direction and is worth doing once as a check: 2500000 bytes a second is 20000000 bits a second on the attacker's link, and 20000000 multiplied by 50 is 10^9, which is the link that was supposed to be filled. The number is worth understanding rather than memorising for two reasons. It quantifies how cheap the attack is, since 2500000 bytes a second is a small fraction of any sending capacity and there are many machines that can produce it, which is why a mitigation that depends on the attacker sending a lot of data is not a mitigation. And it identifies where the defence has to be. Two moves close this particular route, and only one of them is available to the target. The first is to make the responding service return no more than it receives, so the ratio is 1 and the arithmetic collapses; that belongs to whoever operates the responding service, and it is the only measure that helps the wider network. The second is to absorb the excess at the target's own edge, which is what filtering and scrubbing are for and which buys capacity rather than restoring it. The common mistake is to apply a filter and then expect the link to be free, when the filtering is happening behind the link that is already full.
questions.hint: Convert the link to bytes a second first, then divide by the amplification factor.

questions.explanation: The two figures in the question describe two different quantities and the calculation has to convert between them before it can be used. The arrival rate is 300 connections a second, which is a rate. The service time is 250 ms, which is a duration. A service that accepts 300 connections a second and holds each for 0.250 s is holding 300 times 0.25 connections at any instant, which is 75, and 75 is the concurrency the pool has to support. That is the standard relationship between arrival rate, service time and the number in the system, and it is worth using in this direction as often as the reverse because it turns a rate into a capacity requirement, which is the number a deployment decision needs. The second step applies the utilisation target. At 75 concurrent connections the workers would be fully occupied, and fully occupied is the point at which arrival time stops being predictable: a worker that is about to become free is a worker who has not yet been free, so a queue forms and grows with every additional arrival, and the response time is set by the queue rather than by the service time. Targeting 60 per cent means designing for 75 divided by 0.60, which is 125 workers. The margin is not padding, it is what keeps the arrival times bounded when the service time varies, and 40 per cent headroom is a common choice for a service whose work is not perfectly uniform. The same number can be reached the other way round as a check: one worker handling a 250 ms service can retire 4 connections a second, and at 60 per cent utilisation it retires 2.4, and 300 divided by 2.4 is 125. The design consequence is worth stating because it is the part teams miss. This is the pool size for one instance, and the arithmetic has to hold for the peak rather than the average, so a peak factor of three on a mean arrival rate turns the requirement into 375 workers, and a pool that is sized for the average will be the first thing to run out during the peak. It is also the reason a pool that is too large is not free, because every idle connection is a connection the store is holding open.
questions.hint: Convert the arrival rate and the service time into concurrent connections, then divide by the utilisation target.
